qs: tell me about the Aicket repo
a: Aicket is a trainable GPT-style transformer language model built from first principles in Racket, with no PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, NumPy, Hugging Face or CUDA libraries.

qs: what language is Aicket written in
which language does the Aicket repo use
a: Aicket is written in Racket. Its GitHub description is 'ai in racket'.

qs: what is the purpose of Aicket
a: Aicket is a long-term educational systems project: rebuild the deep learning stack layer by layer, document every design decision, and grow it into a working GPT trainer and sampler. It is not a toy or a joke.

qs: why does Aicket build everything from scratch
a: Aicket rebuilds each layer on purpose because most from-scratch GPT projects lean on someone else's tensor library, autograd and tokenizer; Aicket shows how tensors, backprop, optimizers and fast matmul work underneath, in a language with little ML ecosystem.

qs: what is the status of Aicket
a: Aicket: Phases 1-3 are done and Phase 4 (training quality and speed) is in progress. ROADMAP.md is the authoritative checklist; if a capability is not checked off there, assume it does not exist yet.

qs: what does from scratch mean in Aicket
a: In Aicket, 'from scratch' means the ML stack: tensor runtime, autograd, layers, optimizers, tokenizer, dataset/batching, transformer, training loop, inference, and benchmarks. It still uses Racket's standard library and runtime.

qs: how does Aicket handle tensors and autograd
does Aicket have its own autograd
a: Aicket builds its own tensor runtime (shapes, storage, ops) and a reverse-mode autograd engine with a dynamic graph, in both scalar and tensor-level versions.

qs: what is the architecture of the Aicket GPT model
how is the Aicket model built
a: Aicket's GPT has embeddings, causal self-attention with real multi-head attention, LayerNorm, MLP blocks and cross-entropy loss, trained with AdamW using a warmup+decay LR schedule and gradient clipping.

qs: which Aicket implementation should I use
a: Aicket's GPT exists in two parallel implementations: the original scalar-autograd one (single-head only) and a tensor-engine rewrite (tgpt, tcausal-self-attention) with real multi-head attention. The tensor engine is the one to use.

qs: why is Aicket scalar engine kept
a: In Aicket, the scalar-based layer/model/optimizer/train-loop functions are marked DEPRECATED in their own files. They are kept because examples/tiny-char-model.rkt and part of the test suite still use the scalar engine as a teaching artifact.

qs: what training features does Aicket have
a: Aicket's training system includes file-backed datasets, batching, config, checkpointing, CSV loss logging and seeded reproducibility. All are implemented and tested.

qs: how to train the model in Aicket
a: Run Aicket's best demo with 'racket examples/train-only.rkt' and then 'racket examples/infer-only.rkt'. It uses multi-head attention and a ~11.4k-token bundled corpus, and trains in about 12 minutes.

qs: what are the requirements for Aicket
a: Aicket requires Racket (current stable release, no version pinning yet). Run unit tests with 'racket tests/tensor-tests.rkt'; there is no build system beyond raco.

qs: how good is the text Aicket generates
a: Aicket's best demo reproduces exact multi-word entity names from the corpus with zero repetition loops, but text is still garbled at the spelling/word level with no sentence-level coherence. It is explicitly not a real LLM.
Aicket's first real Phase 4 speed result: profiling found matmul's bottleneck was stride recomputation in a generic indexing helper (~89% of time); fixing it gave a measured 7.0-7.6x speedup.

qs: how much faster is the Aicket tensor engine
a: Aicket's tensor engine is about 3.2x faster than its scalar engine, measured with a frozen apples-to-apples comparison of examples/tiny-gpt-train-tensor.rkt versus examples/tiny-gpt-train.rkt.

qs: what training fixes were made in Aicket
a: Aicket's training-quality fixes (2026-07-09, tensor engine): mean-reduced loss, AdamW excluding bias/LayerNorm from weight decay, fan-in-scaled weight init, global-norm gradient clipping, and a warmup+decay LR schedule.

Aicket's known caveats: the MLP uses ReLU instead of GELU; batching sums loss over independently sampled sequences rather than a truly batched forward pass; only matmul has been speed-optimized so far.
Aicket's residual loss noise comes from with-replacement batch sampling over a still-small corpus. The README calls it a data-scale limitation, not a bug, documented in docs/05_optimization.md.

Aicket's source layout: src/ has tensor, autograd, nn, optim, tokenizer, transformer, data, train and infer; plus tests/, examples/, benchmarks/ and docs/. Top-level files include README, ROADMAP, ARCHITECTURE, DESIGN_NOTES, BLOG_NOTES and BENCHMARKS.

qs: what optimizers and tokenizer does Aicket use
a: Aicket's optimizers are SGD and AdamW. Its tokenizer starts char-level and later moves to BPE.
Aicket is intended to become a blog series; see BLOG_NOTES.md and docs/06_blog_outline.md. Long-form docs in docs/ are written to become blog posts.

qs: what is the license of Aicket
a: Aicket's license is listed as TBD. It is developed in public as a learning exercise, and each module has a header comment stating its stage and what is intentionally naive.
Aicket is at github.com/Bobliuuu/Aicket.
Aicket's design decisions and deliberate simplifications are recorded in DESIGN_NOTES.md; system design and module boundaries are in ARCHITECTURE.md; the staged plan is in ROADMAP.md.

qs: how many tests does Aicket have
a: Aicket's tests are run with 'racket tests/*.rkt'; the README says all seven test files pass.

qs: tell me about the chiron repo
a: Chiron is an AI-first community event assistant: users chat to find local nonprofit events or publish a new one.

qs: what language is chiron written in
a: Chiron is written in TypeScript. It is a monorepo using npm workspaces.
Chiron is a monorepo split into a standalone, channel-aware backend and thin frontends. The backend holds all agent and data logic; the web app, voice agent and WhatsApp bot all call it over HTTP.

qs: what folders are in the chiron repo
chiron monorepo apps web server whatsapp
a: Chiron's repo has apps/web (Next.js chat UI), apps/server (Hono backend with agent, events API and Docker), apps/whatsapp (WhatsApp webhook client) and packages/shared (@chiron/shared contract).

qs: what backend framework does chiron use
a: Chiron's backend is a standalone Hono server on Node (apps/server), with routes /api/chat, /api/events and /health, packaged with Docker.
Chiron's web frontend is a thin Next.js chat client (apps/web) that calls the backend over HTTP, showing a ChatApp, event cards and an event creation form.

qs: what does channel-aware mean in chiron
how does chiron differ between web and whatsapp
chiron voice whatsapp email channel behavior
a: Chiron is channel-aware: every /api/chat request carries a channel. On web it offers draft_event, event cards and a prefilled creation form; on voice, whatsapp, email or api it is prose-only and asks clarifying questions.

qs: how does chiron behave on whatsapp
a: On chiron's prose-only channels (voice, whatsapp, email, api) there is no form to render, so the agent asks questions like any LLM, describes results in words, and its actions list is always empty.
Chiron needs Node.js 18.18+ and npm install at the root. Start the backend with 'npm run dev:server' (port 8787) and the web app with 'npm run dev:web' (port 3000).

qs: can chiron run without api keys
a: Chiron runs with zero configuration: with no keys set, the backend uses a deterministic rule-based mock planner and an in-memory seed database, so the whole loop can be demoed immediately.

Chiron's modes: no env uses mock planner plus in-memory events; OPENAI_API_KEY enables an OpenAI tool-calling orchestrator; LOCAL_LLM_ENABLED=true uses a local llama.cpp model; SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_ANON_KEY enable a real events table.
Chiron can use a local GGUF model, Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf, via llama.cpp: run ./scripts/setup-llama.sh, then ./scripts/serve-local-model.sh, with LOCAL_LLM_ENABLED=true.

qs: how does chiron pick an LLM provider
a: Chiron chooses its LLM provider with LLM_PROVIDER (default auto): OpenAI if keyed, else a local model if enabled, else the mock planner. If a live model call fails it falls back to the mock planner so it never hard-fails.

qs: what is the badge in chiron's header
a: Chiron shows a small badge in the web header indicating which LLM and database served each response.

Chiron uses Supabase as its optional database: run supabase/schema.sql (events, profiles, auth, registrations, indexes, RLS policies), optionally supabase/seed.sql, and set the project URL and anon key in apps/server/.env.
Chiron example prompts: 'Find all events in Markham for food banks', 'Recommend me some events', and 'Create an event for a charity fundraiser on June 20th at Cherry St'.

Chiron's backend is packaged with Docker and meant to run on its own behind a custom domain with a Cloudflare DNS-proxied origin. Run it with 'docker compose up --build' (port 8787); see docs/deploy.md.

qs: does chiron have a whatsapp bot
a: Chiron includes a WhatsApp bot (apps/whatsapp) that handles Meta Cloud API webhooks, forwards messages to the backend /api/chat with channel=whatsapp, and keeps per-user conversation history. Run it with 'npm run dev:whatsapp' (port 8788).

qs: what npm scripts does chiron have
a: Chiron's root scripts: dev:server, dev:web, dev:whatsapp, build (backend bundle plus web production build) and typecheck (all workspaces).
Chiron's shared package, @chiron/shared (packages/shared), holds the contract used by every frontend and the backend: channels, chat/agent types and event types.

qs: what is inside chiron's server code
a: Chiron's backend source has src/index.ts (boots @hono/node-server), src/http/app.ts (routes), src/agent/ (orchestrator, tools, prompts, mock planner), src/data/ (Supabase client, events repository, mock store) and src/config.ts.

Chiron's docs: docs/project-overview.md (product vision), docs/architecture.md (how it is wired), docs/deploy.md (Docker and Cloudflare), docs/whatsapp.md (Meta webhook and ngrok), docs/local-model.md.
Chiron is at github.com/Bobliuuu/chiron.

qs: what kind of events does chiron handle
a: Chiron lets users find local nonprofit events and publish new ones through conversation, such as food bank events and charity fundraisers.

qs: tell me about the RAIdology repo
a: RAIdology is an AI-powered radiology assistant that analyzes ultrasound images and presents insights through a chatbot. Its tagline is 'Simplifying radiology, one conversation at a time'.

qs: what language is RAIdology written in
a: RAIdology's GitHub language is listed as Python, with a FastAPI backend and a T3-stack frontend.

RAIdology's objective is a first-line analysis of ultrasound images, focused on the health of the baby and parent, guiding users to a doctor if there are serious issues, and promoting equity by giving accessible care.
RAIdology was inspired by cost: 80 million CT scans a year in the US, up to 1h30 each, is about 120 million physician hours, or roughly 26.04 billion USD a year at 217 USD per hour for a radiologist.

qs: what other ideas did RAIdology consider
a: RAIdology's team considered wildfire prevention, text-to-movie conversion and AI ultrasound detection before choosing the AI ultrasound detection concept.
RAIdology's flow: users reach a landing page, go to a Voiceflow interface, upload ultrasound images, an AI model analyzes them, and an LLM chatbot turns the findings into a simplified overview.

RAIdology's features: a landing page, a Voiceflow interface, ultrasound image upload, an AI analysis model, and an LLM chatbot that answers user queries from the insights. A mobile app is a possibility.
RAIdology's tech stack: T3 stack for the frontend, FastAPI for the backend, Jupyter for inference, and a Lambda Labs A100 GPU instance for training.
RAIdology fine-tuned an ensemble of LLaVa and MiniGPT using QLoRA quantized embeddings. It also researched CLIP to get LLM insights.

RAIdology's production model is a checkpointed MiniGPT fine-tuned on ROCO-instruct to generate medical insights (in tandem with LLaVa-Med), plus a Segment Anything semantic model to detect abscesses and abnormalities.

qs: what hardware did RAIdology train on
a: RAIdology trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU from Lambda Labs. The team would prefer 4x A100 and a 512 SSD as ideal specs for a self fine-tuned large language model.

RAIdology's backend runs a FastAPI endpoint with ReDoc support on a local NVIDIA CUDA deployment, connected to Voiceflow. Image URLs are passed in, inference runs locally, and results go back using the ByteScale API.
RAIdology's backend is deployed on Heroku with Postman and ReDoc, and its frontend is deployed on Voiceflow and Next.JS.
RAIdology uses the Verbwire API to let users mint NFTs on over 13 chains, using the radiology image as the NFT, which can be saved, transacted or sent across chains.

qs: why does RAIdology send NFTs cross chain
a: In RAIdology, sending an NFT cross chain represents sending the image to various hospitals or clinics. Users choose a chain and address, then quick-mint an NFT from a metadata URL via Verbwire.
RAIdology's repo points to: LLaVa (training info and scripts for hosted LLaVa-MED), PAPERS.md (papers used), frontend, backend, and notebooks including a comprehensive Verbwire notebook.

qs: what future features could RAIdology add
a: RAIdology's possible expansions include gestational time estimation, baby size predictions, and recommendations such as whether a C-section might be advisable.

RAIdology's next steps: a mobile version using Voiceflow's mobile optimization, reaching out to clinics and hospitals, better model accuracy, easier onboarding, real-time doctor analysis with funding, and better infrastructure to train LLaVA-Med.

RAIdology's challenges: identifying the precise gap it fills in the medical process (ultrasounds are usually reviewed by a doctor in the office), and continually fine-tuning the AI to interpret ultrasound images.
RAIdology's frontend uses Voiceflow plus Next.js with Tailwind, and the T3 stack. Users are introduced through a landing page and directed to the Voiceflow interface.
RAIdology is at github.com/Bobliuuu/RAIdology.
RAIdology's Verbwire examples are NFTs minted on the Polygon Mumbai testnet, viewable on polygonscan.
RAIdology promotes social equity and inclusion by giving accessible care to users who want their ultrasound or radiology images broken down and explained.

qs: what does the RAIdology chatbot do
a: RAIdology's LLM chatbot converts the AI model's findings from ultrasound images into comprehensive, simplified insights for the user, focused on the health of the carrier.

qs: tell me about the DPass repo
a: DPass is a TypeScript repo whose README is the Next.js with-mongodb example: a Next.js app that connects to MongoDB. The repo has no description of its own.

qs: what language is DPass written in
a: DPass is written in TypeScript.

DPass's README describes MongoDB as a general purpose, document-based, distributed database built for modern application developers and the cloud era; the example shows connecting to it as the backend of a Next.js app.
To run DPass, set up a MongoDB database (local or free MongoDB Atlas), copy .env.local.example to .env.local, set MONGODB_URI, then run 'npm install' and 'npm run dev' (or yarn).

qs: what env variables does DPass need
a: DPass needs one environment variable, MONGODB_URI, the MongoDB connection string; for Atlas it is found via the Connect button on the cluster. Put it in .env.local, which Git ignores.

qs: how do I know DPass is connected to MongoDB
a: DPass runs at http://localhost:3000 in development. It shows 'You are connected to MongoDB' or 'You are NOT connected to MongoDB' depending on whether MONGODB_URI is correct.

qs: how do I bootstrap DPass with create-next-app
a: DPass can be bootstrapped with create-next-app: 'npx create-next-app --example with-mongodb with-mongodb-app' (yarn and pnpm equivalents also work).
DPass can be deployed to Vercel by pushing the project to GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket and importing it, setting the environment variables to match .env.local, or by using the Deploy with Vercel button.
DPass uses the MongoDB Node.js driver; the README points to its docs for querying the database once connected.
DPass is at github.com/Bobliuuu/DPass.
DPass is a Next.js project. For help, the README says to post on Next.js GitHub discussions.

qs: tell me about the EVMElectric repo
a: EVMElectric (also called ElectricEVM in its README) is a web app that lets users crowdsource electric vehicle charging stations using a DAO. Its description: 'Electrifying simple DAO for crowdsourcing charging stations'.

qs: what language is EVMElectric written in
a: EVMElectric's GitHub language is listed as Cadence (Flow's smart contract language); the backend is Node.js and TypeScript, with Fastify and Flask endpoints.

EVMElectric was inspired by the difficulty of finding EV charging stations, which can offset the benefit of owning an electric vehicle. The team hopes to foster the next generation of electric vehicles.

qs: what can users do in EVMElectric
a: In EVMElectric, users can add charging stations, view existing stations on a map or web view, and use wallet features such as viewing balances, minting NFTs, or running smart contracts with emulation.
EVMElectric includes a Voiceflow LLM that answers questions about the app and about sustainability and blockchain topics.

EVMElectric uses Hedera: the Hedera Consensus Service (HCS) logs payments, the HBAR wallet via the SDK validates balances and creates crypto payments, and the Hedera File Service (HFS) uploads and downloads files via the Fastify API.
EVMElectric uses Flow's emulator and playground to mint and deploy NFTs, translated from Solidity to Cadence, using Flow wallets and a service to help new users onboard and mint.
EVMElectric uses Verbwire to take NFT metadata and send it cross chain to other chains so it can be viewed on OpenSea.

EVMElectric's stack: Streamlit and Matplotlib frontend; Node.js and TypeScript backend with Fastify and Flask endpoints connected via Axios and requests; Verbwire, Hedera SDK, Flow Emulator, Hardhat and Alchemy; Voiceflow with GPT-4.

qs: what blockchain tools does EVMElectric use
a: EVMElectric uses Hardhat and Alchemy to deploy Solidity scripts, and emulators including the Flow emulator, Hardhat and Hedera Testnet for wallet and smart contract activity.

EVMElectric's challenges: connecting frontend and backend while new to Solidity and Cadence, learning Hedera services, implementing heatmaps, issues with Flow (so they emulated it), and quick micropayments validated with HCS.
EVMElectric's team is proud of a working demo and backend that combines blockchain and full stack principles, and that it was their first time using Flow.

qs: what did EVMElectric teach its builders
a: EVMElectric's team learned about Hedera, Flow and DAO principles, and that HCS and HFS are a very cheap alternative to tools like IPFS and decentralized logging. They hope to add zk-proofs and rollups.
EVMElectric's next steps: add more features and improve the onboarding process for new users, to onboard the next generation of electric vehicles.
EVMElectric was built as a hackathon project; its last push was in September 2023.
EVMElectric is at github.com/Bobliuuu/EVMElectric.

qs: what is the DAO in EVMElectric
a: EVMElectric uses a DAO so users can crowdsource charging stations in order to complete purchases.
